Opinion writer Alejandro Barbosa believes the recent sabotage attacks are something to be concerned about. (Sofiia Gatilova | REUTERS) By Alejandro Barbosa , Opinion Writer Oct 5, 2026 On the night of Aug. 5 at Leipzig/Halle airport in eastern Germany, a drone carrying an explosive device was found near an aircraft belonging to Ukrainian carrier Antonov Airlines. This aircraft was carrying munitions bound for Ukraine. The airport, one of Europe’s main cargo hubs, was partly shut down. About a month later, on Sept. 1, the German government blamed Russia for the incident. However, this is not an isolated incident. Since Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022, the Kremlin has supported sabotage campaigns throughout Europe meant to undermine support for Ukraine . In recent months, these incidents have intensified and become more frequent. A little over a week later, on Aug. 15, a fire believed to be an arson attack occurred at a building in Estonia used by Milrem Robotics. This defense company manufactures and provides military vehicles used in Ukraine. According to a Sept. 29 Associated Press article, the Estonian government concluded Russian security agencies commissioned the incident as an act of sabotage. According to an Associated Press article from December 2025 that mapped notable sabotage incidents throughout the war up to that point, there had been 145 incidents attributed to Russia since the 2022 invasion began. In November 2025, a sabotage incident occurred in Poland in which an explosive device detonated and damaged a railway line, according to a New York Times article. On the same line, a damaged overhead line caused a passenger train carrying 475 people to abruptly stop. The Polish government blamed Russian security services for the attack. Although these incidents may seem like they only affect Europe, some of America’s most important allies, notably the U.K. and Germany, are in Europe. Ukraine also relies heavily on American support, including billions of dollars ’ worth of weapons such as Patriot defense systems and humanitarian aid since 2022. For America to ignore these developments would risk allowing Russia to further undermine European security. David Agaton, a sophomore majoring in public health, believes the war in Ukraine is detrimental. “It is a war; people are dying, and it is still ongoing since, I don’t know how long, and it is still pretty bad,” Agaton said. As the so-called “leader of the free world,” the United States, has an obligation to help Ukraine and European allies defend themselves and make it crystal clear to Russian President Vladimir Putin that the U.S. will defend its allies if their territorial integrity is threatened, as shown by NATO’s article 5 and the Budapest Memorandum, the latter being violated by Russia, who was a signatory. Despite President Donald Trump’s apparent disinterest in Ukraine, on Sept. 19 he signed a new sanctions bill into law to further hold Russia accountable for its invasion. Many European countries are preparing for more frequent and intense attacks. Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk, for example, has said Poland must prepare for more acts of sabotage, including possibly drone attacks. These incidents are not something the U.S. can simply brush off as a European affair. The U.S. also has military bases throughout the region, notably in Germany. If Russia is willing to target Poland and Estonia, why wouldn’t it attack Germany again or even try to attack the U.K.? Russia has already been accused of targeting Germany, so what would prevent attacks against U.S. military installations in Europe? These recent sabotage attacks are something to be concerned about, or at the very least, something to take seriously.
